news.title: A Bad Browser Add-On Can Now Act As You in Chrome or Edge — Remove Add-Ons You Don't Recognize
news.excerpt: Bad add-ons for the program you use to go on the internet can now take over the smart helper built into it. Researchers showed one add-on — installed like any other — letting the helper read files, open pages, and act as the person using it, with no click at all. No fake page and no scam message to spot, because the add-on is really installed. Fix it in two minutes: open your browser's menu, find the list of add-ons, and remove anything you don't recognize.

news.title: Scammers Are Cashing In on a Real Government Refund — Don't Fall for It
news.excerpt: A real refund program is sending money to people who got signed up for a subscription they didn't want — and crooks are already using the news to trick folks out of their bank details. The Federal Trade Commission says it will never call, text, or email you to offer a refund, and never asks you to pay a fee to collect. If you get a message about money you're owed, that's a scam. Don't reply and don't click. Go to ftc.gov/refunds and look up the program yourself.

news.title: That 'Your Parcel Couldn't Be Delivered — Pay $4.95' Message Is Fake
news.excerpt: A fresh batch of fake messages says a parcel couldn't be delivered and you owe about five dollars to get it moving. The link opens a page that copies the post office's official look, then asks for your name, your phone number, and finally your bank card. That's an email scam, not a shipping notice. The real Postal Service, UPS, and FedEx never text a link for a small fee. Don't click — open the carrier's real website and check your tracking number there.

news.title: Those 'Your Rewards Points Are Expiring' Texts Are Fake
news.excerpt: A wave of fake text messages is telling people their rewards points are about to expire, with a believable balance and a deadline to make it feel urgent. The link inside opens a fake sign-in page that steals your email address and password. Researchers counted more than a thousand versions of the same message. Don't use the link. Open the company's official website instead by typing its address into your browser, then sign in there and check for yourself.

news.title: That Antivirus Renewal Email Is Fake — Check Your Bank Statement First
news.excerpt: Scammers are emailing people a convincing receipt that says their antivirus subscription just auto-renewed for about $130, with a handy link to cancel it. There is no subscription and no charge. The cancel page is a fake form that collects your name, email address and number so a fake support agent can call you next. Don't click the link and don't fill in that form. Check your own bank statement instead — no charge means nothing to cancel.

posts.title: Microsoft's September Windows update muted the sound and froze games on some PCs — get the free emergency patch in Settings > Windows Update
posts.summary: Microsoft's big September Windows update has been rough on a small number of computers — people reported speakers and headsets going silent, a black screen after signing in, and games freezing. Microsoft has already released a free emergency patch. Click Start, then open Settings > Windows Update and click Check for updates; install everything it offers and restart. If your sound or screen is still dead afterward, you can undo just that one change: Settings > Windows Update > Update history > Uninstall updates.
posts.truth: The honest answer is one you might not expect from a repair shop: don't skip this update. It closed about a thousand security holes, and "waiting it out" is how people get hurt. The trouble that made the news hit a small slice of machines, mostly gaming computers, and Microsoft patched the worst of it within days. The pattern I see over and over is the same — the folks who install their updates calmly stay out of trouble, and the ones who ignore them for a year are the ones who end up paying me. Update, then use your computer as normal.

posts.title: Criminals are selling scans of 153 million driver's licenses — freeze your credit free with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion
posts.summary: A dark-web service is selling digital scans of more than 153 million driver's licenses from the U.S. and Canada, and the FBI has opened an investigation. You can't un-leak a license, but you can lock your credit so nobody opens a loan or a card in your name. Go to equifax.com, experian.com, and transunion.com, sign up for a free account, and click Freeze — do all three, because it's free by law and takes about ten minutes total. If you'd rather see your reports first, go to annualcreditreport.com, the one government-approved site for free reports.
posts.truth: Most people think a credit freeze stops them from using their own credit. It doesn't. A freeze only stops new accounts from being opened in your name — you can unfreeze it in about a minute from your phone when you're buying a car or a house. I see people freeze one bureau and think they're done. You need all three, because a lender is only required to check one, and the crook will pick the one you forgot. The honest answer: a freeze is the single most effective thing an ordinary person can do after a leak like this, and it costs nothing.

posts.title: Your computer's drive can warn you before it quits — Windows 11 shows its free health report in Settings > System > Storage
posts.summary: Click Start, type Storage, and open Storage settings. Then click Advanced storage settings, then Disks & volumes, click the drive your files live on, click Properties, and read the Drive health line. If it says Healthy, you're fine. If it says Caution or Bad, that drive is on its way out — copy what you can't lose onto something else today, not next month.
posts.truth: Most people think their photos and paperwork die when the computer dies. They don't. They die when the little drive inside the computer dies, and that drive almost always tells you it's failing weeks ahead of time — a slowdown here, a weird clicking or grinding sound there, a warning that's been sitting in Settings that nobody ever opened. The honest answer is that a $60 replacement today is a lot cheaper than $400 to a data recovery lab later. I've never once had a customer tell me they wished they'd waited. I also install and open CrystalDiskInfo — free from crystalmark.info — and read the one-word health status and the drive's temperature.

posts.title: Stop ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude from training their AI on your chats — three free settings, about two minutes each
posts.summary: In ChatGPT, open Settings → Data Controls and turn off Improve the model for everyone. In Gemini, open Settings and turn off Keep Activity (or go to myactivity.google.com and turn off Gemini Apps Activity). In Claude, open Settings → Privacy and turn off the model improvement setting. Nothing breaks when you do this and nothing costs money — you keep using the app exactly as before, and your conversations stop feeding the next version of it.
posts.truth: People tell me, "I only ask it silly stuff, who cares." Most people don't realize the chats that really matter are the ones you'd never say out loud: helping word a letter to your doctor, pasting in a bill to figure out a charge, typing in your own address to fill out a form. That's exactly the material that gets kept and reviewed. The honest answer is that a chatbot is a conversation with a company, not a conversation with a friend. You can still use it every single day and tell it not to take notes.

posts.title: Is your Windows 11 computer about to stop getting free security updates? Microsoft's October 13 deadline takes 30 seconds to check in Settings
posts.summary: On October 13, Microsoft stops sending free security updates to the older version of Windows 11 that shipped back in 2024. The fix is free and it's just an update: open Settings > Windows Update, click Check for updates, and install everything it offers — your files and programs stay exactly where they are. Not sure which version you have? Press the Start button and type About your PC; it's written right there in plain text.
posts.truth: Updates feel like nagging, so people put them off — and then they get used to the nagging. Most people don't realize that once a version of Windows stops getting updates, every new flaw the bad guys find from that day forward stays open forever. Nothing warns you. One morning the computer is simply easier to break into than it was the day before. The honest answer is that the newest free version of Windows 11 is the safest one, and getting it costs you one evening at home with a cup of coffee and a progress bar.

posts.title: Your colorful gaming keyboard or mouse can crash your games — Microsoft says unplug it and update the lights app (Corsair iCUE, Razer Synapse, or Logitech G HUB)
posts.summary: Microsoft traced a wave of game freezes and blue screens to the software that runs the colored lights on keyboards, mice, and headsets. If your games suddenly hang or crash, unplug the light-up accessory and restart — if the crashing stops, that accessory is your culprit. Then open the app that controls it (Corsair iCUE, Razer Synapse, Logitech G HUB, MSI Center, or ASUS Armoury Crate) and run its update, or uninstall it and let the device fall back to its built-in colors. It's free either way.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize the pretty lights come with a program that reaches deep inside Windows — much deeper than it ever needs to. The lights themselves are harmless; the app behind them is what fights with games. And here's the part nobody tells you: if a friend or a grandkid built your gaming computer and loaded five different lighting apps on it, that's the machine that's going to act up. One lighting app is plenty. If you never touch the colors anyway, removing the app costs you nothing at all.

posts.title: Windows 11's Recall takes a picture of your screen every few seconds — turn it off free in Settings > Privacy & security > Recall & snapshots
posts.summary: On newer "Copilot+" Windows 11 computers, a feature called Recall quietly saves snapshots of everything on your screen so you can search your own history later. Most people never turned it on and never agreed to it. To check: click Start, type Recall & snapshots, and open Settings > Privacy & security > Recall & snapshots. Turn off Save snapshots — or click Pause and delete what's already saved. If the setting isn't there, your computer simply doesn't have it, and you're done.
posts.truth: The honest answer is that Recall isn't evil — it's a camera roll of your screen, and that roll includes your bank page, your e-mail, and whatever the grandkids sent you. The problem is that if anyone ever gets into your computer, they get all of it in one place. Most people don't realize it's on by default on those machines. I turn it off unless a customer specifically asks for it, because in all this time, not one person has come back and said, "I wish you'd left it on."

posts.title: Windows 11's free September update lets you move the taskbar to the top of the screen and shut Bing off in Search — get it at Settings > Windows Update
posts.summary: Install it from Settings > Windows Update and restart. Then, to move the taskbar: Settings > Personalization > Taskbar > Taskbar behaviors > Taskbar position, and pick Left, Top, Right, or Bottom. There's also a smaller taskbar size in that same section if the bar feels too tall. To stop the Start menu from covering half your screen: Settings > Personalization > Start > Start menu size, and choose Small. To make Search instant and quiet: Settings > Privacy & security > Search, open Show suggested search results, and turn off Web Searches and Microsoft Store suggestions.
posts.truth: I see this all the time — folks who came off Windows 10 and never got comfortable on Windows 11, and it's almost always the same two complaints: the taskbar is nailed to the bottom of the screen, and the Start menu covers everything. For five years Microsoft said no. This month they finally said yes, and it didn't cost a thing. Most people don't realize the updates they keep clicking past are where the good stuff hides. The honest answer: the biggest improvement to your computer this year arrived free, and it took one restart.

posts.title: Update Firefox free to get a PDF reader that opens up to 45% faster — click Menu, then Help, then About Firefox
posts.summary: The newest Firefox came out September 15, and Mozilla says the PDF reader built into it now starts up to 45% faster, with a big drop in memory and processor use when a page is showing large photos. To get it: open Firefox, click the Menu button (the three lines in the top right corner), then Help, then About Firefox. It checks and installs the newest version for free, and your tabs, bookmarks, and saved passwords all stay exactly where they are.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize they're reading their power bills, insurance papers, and lab results in a PDF reader that came free inside their web browser — so upgrading the browser upgrades the reader. I watch folks email a document to themselves just to open it on another machine because the one on the desk feels slow. The honest answer is that a browser update isn't housekeeping you can skip. It's the single easiest thing you can do for both speed and safety at the same time, and it costs you one click and a restart.

posts.title: Columbia County's library pays for Career Online High School — a free, accredited high school diploma you finish from your kitchen table
posts.summary: Call the Columbia County Public Library at (386) 758-2111 and ask about Career Online High School. It's a real, accredited high school diploma plus a career certificate, done entirely online at your own pace, and the grant pays the whole cost — you don't pay a dime. The library has a page with the enrollment steps on columbiacountyfla.com (search "Career Online High School" on the site).
posts.truth: Most folks who never finished school assume that door closed a long time ago, and that going back means sitting in a classroom with teenagers and taking a test you won't pass. The honest answer is neither of those is true anymore. This is the same accredited diploma, from your own house, on your own hours — an hour after supper, or Sunday morning before church. The library does the paperwork and picks up the bill. I see people in this shop every week who make a good living with their hands and still feel like that missing diploma is hanging over them. It isn't too late, and it isn't expensive. It's free.
